volumes.title: A Book Coming Apart
volumes.text:
The Statute Book of Emberwick has lost its spine, two corners and most of its dignity. The council has therefore asked me, Hesper Quill, Borough Clerk, to copy all forty-one statutes fresh, and to set beside each a plain account of how it came to be made.

I begin with Statute One: that no goods be sold in the market before the market bell has rung. It dates from the morning a fishmonger from the Grey Coast sold his whole cart of herring to one innkeeper before dawn, and the town breakfasted on porridge and resentment.

One oddity already. The page for Statute Seventeen is blank. The index, in a hand far older than mine, says only: "Seventeen. See the mace." I have seen the mace. It is a brass stick with a knob on it. I shall look again.

volumes.title: The Goose Hour
volumes.text:
Statute Four, which I, Hesper Quill, Borough Clerk, have this week copied into the new Statute Book, provides that geese may be driven along Tanner's Row only between six and seven in the morning.

The cause was the wet summer of Mayor Pollard's year. His procession, with band, turned into Tanner's Row from the north at the moment two hundred geese bound for the Lowlands market entered it from the south. Neither party would give way. The geese, being more numerous and less embarrassed, prevailed. The mayor's hat was recovered from the river Ember a week later and is kept in the town hall, in a case.

The statute has never once been broken, chiefly because geese prefer the early hour. I record it as a rare instance of a law that agrees with those it governs.

volumes.title: Lanterns on Bridge Street
volumes.text:
In recopying the borough's statutes I come to the Ninth, and I, Hesper Quill, Clerk of Emberwick, confess it is my favourite. On any night of marsh fog, each household in Bridge Street shall hang a lit lantern at its door until morning.

It was made after a carter named Jeb Marlow, feeling his way home, mistook the river for the road. He and the horse were fished out unharmed, though a load of turnips went on to the sea. The street met next evening in the cooper's yard and agreed the rule among themselves. The council merely wrote it down a year later and took the credit.

That is the usual order of things, I find. The town decides, and the statute arrives afterwards, slightly out of breath. On foggy nights I walk down to count the lanterns, eleven of them, and feel well governed.

volumes.title: No Whistling by the Weir
volumes.text:
Statute Twelve forbids whistling within fifty paces of the weir after dusk. Strangers to Emberwick suppose it a joke. As Borough Clerk, copying the old Statute Book page by page, I can report that it is nothing of the kind.

The lock-keeper of that day signalled to the night barges by whistle: one long note for wait, two short for come on. A baker's boy, walking home pleased with himself and whistling a jig, delivered what amounted to nine contradictory orders. Two barges met in the cut. Nobody was hurt, but forty sacks of flour went into the water, and the ducks below the weir grew noticeably stout.

The keeper now uses a lamp, so the reason has gone. The statute stays. I have marked it "kept for the sake of the story", which is not a legal category, but ought to be.

volumes.title: The Brass Loaf
volumes.text:
Statute Fourteen: every baker in Emberwick shall keep a loaf-board of the borough's pattern, and no penny loaf shall be smaller than the board. I, Hesper Quill, Borough Clerk, copy it out with the smell of bread at my window.

Two bakers, Orrin and Padbury, once faced each other across Cheap Street. Each meant to be the cheaper, and managed it by making the loaf a little smaller every week. By midsummer a penny loaf could be lost in a coat pocket. The council had one honest loaf cast in brass and hung it in the town hall.

Mrs. Padbury's daughter Nell, who is eight, asked me what a statute was. A promise the whole town makes, I said. She asked who checks. I said that I do. She looked at me as one looks at a very small dog set to guard a very large house.

volumes.title: The Blank Page
volumes.text:
I have reached the page that should hold Statute Seventeen, and it holds nothing. The index of the old Statute Book says, "Seventeen. See the mace." So this morning I, Hesper Quill, Borough Clerk, went and saw the mace.

Mr. Corriby, the mace-bearer, lifted it from its case with both hands. It is brass, as long as a walking stick, with a head like a turnip. I read every inch of it through my glass. There is the borough's ember, a date, a dent from the procession of the wet summer, and no statute at all.

"It rattles a bit," said Mr. Corriby, shaking it gently. "Always has. A loose pin, my father thought." I agreed it was probably a pin. In the new book I have left a clean page with the number at the top, which looks either hopeful or foolish.

volumes.title: Cats of the Corn Exchange
volumes.text:
Statute Twenty requires the borough to maintain not fewer than three cats at the Corn Exchange, their wages to be paid in fish each Friday. I, Hesper Quill, Clerk, copying it into the new Statute Book, find it faithfully observed for a hundred and sixty years.

It followed the Mouse Autumn, when the grain merchants of the Lowlands threatened to take their trade elsewhere. One merchant opened a sample sack before a buyer and three mice climbed out, in no hurry. The council acted within the week, which for the council is a gallop.

The present officers are Dimity, Burdock and the Chancellor. Their names stand in the ledger between the lamplighter and the man who winds the clock. I took Friday's herring down myself. The Chancellor accepted it without thanks, as is the way of those long in office.

volumes.title: Washing and the High Street
volumes.text:
No person shall hang washing across the High Street on a market day. So runs Statute Twenty-Three, and in copying it I, the Borough Clerk of Emberwick, went looking for the reason, as the council has asked me to do for all forty-one.

The reason was a bedsheet. The households on either side of the High Street once shared lines strung between their upper windows. Then, one gusty market morning, a double sheet belonging to a Mrs. Arkle came loose and descended upon a string of wool-merchants' ponies. The ponies concluded that the sky had fallen. The damage was mostly to cheeses.

What I admire is the wording. The council did not forbid the lines, only the market day. Six days in seven the street still flies its shirts like flags. A law may be exactly as large as the trouble, and no larger.

volumes.title: The Ferryman's Oath
volumes.text:
Each New Year the ferryman of the Ember comes to my office, lays his hand on the Statute Book, and swears not to charge more in rain than in shine. That is Statute Twenty-Eight. This year he swore on the old book, while the fresh copy I am making lay drying beside it.

The law remembers a ferryman called Dunstan Gaule, who kept two prices and a sharp eye on the clouds. In a downpour the fare doubled. In a thunderstorm it was whatever you had. The council took the view that weather is nobody's merchandise.

The present ferryman, Jory, asked what I, the Clerk, was frowning at. I showed him the blank page for Statute Seventeen and the old index. "See the mace," he read. "Well, have you tried looking in it, and not at it?" I told him a mace is not a cupboard.

volumes.title: The Lamp in the Window
volumes.text:
Statute Thirty-Three concerns the library, and so I, Hesper Quill, Borough Clerk, copied it there, at the long table, to be among its beneficiaries. It orders that a lamp be kept burning in the library window until the last reader has gone home.

The cause was a schoolmaster, Mr. Evander Loom, who sat down one winter afternoon with a history of the Northern Fells and looked up to find the doors locked, the stove out and the hour past midnight. He spent the night wrapped in the reading-room curtain and finished the book. He bore no grudge, but asked the council for some sign that somebody knew he was there.

So the lamp is less a light than a promise. While it burns, you are not forgotten. The night shelver trims it still. I finished my page by it, and she waited, and did not hurry me.

volumes.title: Telling the Bees
volumes.text:
The last statute, the Forty-First, directs that the borough's bees be told the name of each new mayor. I, Hesper Quill, Clerk, have now copied it, and with it every law of Emberwick except the Seventeenth, whose page is blank and whose index entry says only, "See the mace."

A mayor was once installed without the almshouse hives being informed, and that summer they swarmed to the next parish. The council thought it cheaper to tell them than to find out.

Today Mr. Corriby brought the mace to my office for its mayor-making polish. He worked at the head with a cloth, turning as he rubbed, and the head turned with him. It came off in his hand like the lid of a jar. We both looked into the hollow. There was no loose pin. There was a small roll of paper, tied with thread.

volumes.title: Statute Seventeen
volumes.text:
The paper that rattled inside the borough mace for generations is the lost Statute Seventeen. I, Hesper Quill, Clerk of Emberwick, have copied it onto its page: "Once in each generation the Clerk shall read every statute aloud to a child under ten, and shall strike out whichever one the child cannot be made to understand."

So I read all forty-one to Nell Padbury, the baker's daughter, who is eight. She approved the goose hour, the lanterns in the fog and the cats' wages. She stuck fast on Statute Thirty, which forbids any person to be "unreasonably prominent" at the autumn fair. I explained it three ways. I could not explain it to myself.

It is struck out. The new book holds forty statutes, each understood by at least one citizen. I have put the paper back inside the mace. I have grown fond of the rattle.

volumes.title: The Goose in the Dock
volumes.text:
The Petty Sessions of Emberwick sit in the Moot Room above the market hall, and there, one Tuesday in October, Magistrate Dorcas Thrale heard the case of Larkin against a goose.

The goose, Admiral, owned by Mrs. Hobb, was accused of entering Mr. Larkin's garden and eating most of a marrow meant for the Harvest Fair. Mr. Larkin produced the stalk. Mrs. Hobb produced the goose, which was a mistake. Admiral left his basket, crossed the floor and struck the witness box such a blow that one of its feet snapped off. The usher, Mr. Fenn, restored order and, during the adjournment, the box.

Mrs. Hobb is to supply Mr. Larkin with goose eggs until the next fair. When the magistrate reached for her gavel to close the sitting, it was not on the bench. She rapped with her knuckles. The gavel has not been seen since.

volumes.title: The Leaning Gatepost
volumes.text:
At the Emberwick Petty Sessions, before Magistrate Thrale, Simeon Dray, carter, was charged with knocking down the north gatepost of the almshouses with a wagon of coal.

Dray's defence was that the post had been leaning into the lane for years and had at last leaned into him. The court adjourned to look: the magistrate, the usher, six almswomen and a dog. The fallen post could say nothing for itself, but its fellow on the south side was found to lean at a most suggestive angle. A plumb line was borrowed from the mason and hung beside it.

It was held that the post had contributed. Dray is to set both upright, the borough supplying mortar. The court's gavel being still missing since the goose's trial, the magistrate closed with a wooden spoon lent by the caretaker. It made a homely sound, and nobody felt very sentenced.

volumes.title: The Disputed Pie
volumes.text:
The Harvest Fair gave the Emberwick bench its sweetest case. Two pies stood side by side on the judging table, the first-prize ticket fell off in a draught, and both Mrs. Quennell and Mr. Abner Stout swore the winner was theirs.

Magistrate Thrale had the pie brought into the Moot Room, with a lump of dough from the baker. Each claimant was asked to crimp a strip of pastry before the court. Mrs. Quennell pinched hers with a thumb and two fingers. Mr. Stout pressed his with a fork. The edge of the prize pie was plainly forked. Mr. Stout wept a little.

Mrs. Quennell took it handsomely and asked for his recipe, which was refused. The pie, being evidence, was then eaten by the court, and this reporter can confirm the judges' opinion. The sitting was closed with a darning mushroom, the gavel being still lost.

volumes.title: Thirteen at Midnight
volumes.text:
On the ninth of November the town clock of Emberwick struck thirteen at midnight and woke all Bridge Street. The sexton, Mr. Obadiah Crane, who has charge of the clock, was brought before Magistrate Thrale for a public nuisance.

Eleven witnesses had counted thirteen. A twelfth counted fourteen, but admitted to being asleep for the first. Mr. Crane said he had been in bed, and that the clock strikes by itself, which is the whole merit of a clock. The clockmaker, called as an expert, had climbed the tower and found feathers on the striking hammer. An owl had been sitting on it. When the owl left, the hammer fell once more.

Mr. Crane was discharged. The owl was held to be beyond the reach of the court. The magistrate, whose gavel is still missing, closed by rapping a brass door knocker on the bench.

volumes.title: The Ladder of Nine Houses
volumes.text:
Eleven years ago Mr. Hale of Emberwick lent his ladder to a neighbour, to clear a gutter. It has since passed through nine households, and at these Petty Sessions he asked Magistrate Thrale for it back. Mrs. Tibb, who has it now, said she had it honestly from the Pococks.

Nine witnesses were called. Each had borrowed the ladder "only for the afternoon". The witness box bore all nine within the hour, some of them substantial, without a tremor. The magistrate remarked that the usher, Mr. Fenn, had made a fine job of mending it after the goose broke its foot. Mr. Fenn studied the ceiling.

Ruling: the ladder has become the town's by custom. It is to hang at the pump, with a slate for names, and Mr. Hale has first turn. The sitting closed with a cobbler's last. The gavel remains at large.

volumes.title: Half a Ferry Crossing
volumes.text:
Jory, ferryman of the Ember, came before the Emberwick bench to claim twopence from Mr. Lucius Pennyfold, a traveller in buttons. The river being low, the ferry had grounded in midstream, and Mr. Pennyfold had waded the rest. He offered a penny: half the fare for half the crossing.

Jory answered that he had waded too, with Mr. Pennyfold's sample case on his head, and that not one button was wet. Magistrate Thrale held that the bargain was to be put on the far bank, and that Mr. Pennyfold had been, though damp to the knee. The fare was owed in full. The ferryman, however, must pay for the drying of the stockings, assessed at twopence.

So the twopence crossed the bench twice and ended where it began, and both men left satisfied. She closed with a pepper mill, the gavel being still lost, and sneezed.

volumes.title: The Scarecrow's Sunday Coat
volumes.text:
Mr. Dunmore's best coat was found on a scarecrow in Gedge's bean field, and Kit Hatch, the farm boy, aged twelve, was charged before Magistrate Thrale at the Emberwick sessions with taking it.

Kit said the coat had been handed to him at the Dunmores' back door, for the scarecrow, with a slice of cake. Mr. Dunmore called this an invention. Mrs. Dunmore was called. She looked at her husband from the witness box and said that the coat was twenty years old and green at the seams, that she had asked him since spring, and that the cake was seed cake.

No theft was found. The coat is to stay on the scarecrow, which it fits. Mr. Dunmore is to be measured for a new one, by order not of the court but of Mrs. Dunmore. The sitting closed with a rolling pin, the gavel being still absent.

volumes.title: The Swarm in Dispute
volumes.text:
In June a swarm of bees left Miss Pargeter's hive in Emberwick and settled in Mr. Odd's pear tree, two gardens away. Mr. Odd hived them. Miss Pargeter wanted them back, and the matter came before Magistrate Thrale.

The custom of the borough is old: a swarm stays yours while you follow it, ringing a pan, and never lose sight of it. Miss Pargeter had followed, ringing a pan, but owned that she lost sight of the bees while climbing a wall. Mr. Odd said a wall was a wall. The magistrate said that custom asks for reasonable pursuit and does not require a beekeeper to fly.

The bees go home to Miss Pargeter. Mr. Odd receives the first comb of honey for his trouble. The court's gavel being still missing, the sitting was closed by striking the pan itself, which was heard in the market.

volumes.title: The Snow Magistrate
volumes.text:
In January the beadle of Emberwick marched five children up to the Moot Room, charged with disrespect to the bench. They had built a snow figure outside the market hall, with a coal frown and a wig of sheep's wool, and it was unmistakably Magistrate Thrale.

The magistrate went down to view the accused. She walked round it twice. The likeness, she said, was fair, though she did not believe she was so wide. A portrait is no offence. The hat, however, was poor, and they were to find a better. They did. The snow magistrate stood until the thaw.

The sitting closed with a toy mallet lent by the youngest defendant, Posy Hatch, aged five, who asked for a receipt. She wondered aloud if the court would ever see its own gavel again. The usher, Mr. Fenn, said he had looked everywhere a gavel ought to be.

volumes.title: The Weathercock's Word
volumes.text:
Mr. Silas Gurney, a fisherman of the Grey Coast, sued the borough of Emberwick at the Petty Sessions. Before setting out he had consulted the weathercock on the market hall, which promised a fair south-westerly. He was soaked to the skin by ten o'clock and lost a day's catch.

The borough pleaded that a weathercock is an ornament and promises nothing. A steeplejack, sent up the roof, reported that the bird was rusted solid and had pointed south-west since the spring before last. Magistrate Thrale held that a thing set on a public roof to tell the wind must tell it or come down.

The borough is to oil the weathercock. Mr. Gurney is awarded a dry coat from the lost-property cupboard. The gavel being still missing, the magistrate closed with a lead fishing weight lent by the plaintiff. The wind has since been reported as changeable.

volumes.title: The Admiral Returns
volumes.text:
A year after his first trial the goose Admiral was found one morning inside the Moot Room of Emberwick, having climbed the stairs alone. He was sitting beneath the witness box, pecking at one of its feet. His owner, Mrs. Hobb, was summoned for letting him stray.

Magistrate Thrale asked what a goose could want with a witness box. Mr. Aske, the carpenter, who was waiting on another matter, knelt to look. He reported that one leg of the box was two inches short and stood upon "something that is not a wedge". The usher, Mr. Fenn, went pink.

The goose was dismissed with a caution. Mr. Aske is to bring his tools to the next sessions and lift the box. The magistrate closed with her knuckles, as on the day the court's gavel first went missing, and looked for some time at her usher.

volumes.title: The Matter of the Gavel
volumes.text:
For a year the Emberwick bench has been called to order with spoons and door knockers, the gavel having vanished the day a goose broke the foot of the witness box. Today Mr. Aske, the carpenter, lifted the box. Under its short leg lay the gavel.

The usher, Mr. Fenn, came forward unasked. He had wanted something of the right height, only for the afternoon, and had meant to mention it. Since then every witness in the borough had sworn to tell the truth standing on top of it.

Magistrate Thrale tried the matter on the spot. She found Mr. Fenn guilty of good intentions and sentenced him to buns for the court. The box is to have a proper foot. Then she rapped the gavel, which is worn flat on one side and no longer rolls off the bench. She called it improved by its year of service.

volumes.title: To Whoever Sits Here
volumes.text:
I have been magistrate of Emberwick for thirty-one years, and at the Midwinter Sessions I shall stop. The council has not yet told me who follows. So I write to a stranger, and shall leave this book in the bench drawer of the Moot Room, under the spare candles.

Nobody gave me a companion when I began. I was handed a key, a gavel and a list of fines, and left to learn the rest by doing it wrong in public. You may be spared a little of that.

First counsel, then. Come early on your first morning, before the stove is lit, and sit for five minutes on the public's back bench. Look at the magistrate's chair from there. Notice how far away it is, and how high. That is how you will look to them. Remember it when you are up there feeling ordinary.

volumes.title: On Hearing People Out
volumes.text:
Let them finish. I, Dorcas Thrale, have sat on the Emberwick bench long enough to promise you, my successor, that this is the hardest rule and the most useful.

People do not bring their trouble out in order. They begin with the grievance they have rehearsed. The real matter comes last, usually after "and another thing". A man once stood before me for twenty minutes complaining of his neighbour's cockerel. I had the poultry by-law open and my finger on the place. Then he said, "And another thing, since my wife died there is nobody to grumble to when it wakes me." There is no by-law for that.

I adjourned and spoke to the neighbour, who now takes him a brown egg most mornings. The cockerel crows as before. Had I ruled at the tenth minute I should have been perfectly correct, and no use at all.

volumes.title: On the Chair
volumes.text:
The magistrate's chair you inherit in the Moot Room of Emberwick was made for a Justice Harbottle, who stood six feet four. I am five feet one. For thirty-one years my feet have not touched the floor during sessions.

It is a piece of furniture. It makes whoever sits in it look certain, and the danger is that it works on the sitter too. On the first morning I felt I deserved its height, I fined a pedlar for having no licence, though plainly he had been robbed of it. My conscience reversed me by supper, and I repaid him from my own purse.

I keep a cushion on the seat, embroidered by my sister with a goose. It is for comfort. It also reminds me, whenever I sit to judge my neighbours, that I am sitting on a goose. I shall leave it for you.

volumes.title: On Fines and Mending
volumes.text:
You will be handed the borough's list of fines on your first day as Emberwick's magistrate. I, Dorcas Thrale, set this beside it. Fine people in a coin they can find. A fine a poor man cannot pay is only a debt, and a debt brings him back before you.

Better still, where you can, give a sentence that mends the thing broken. A boy once swung on the handle of the town pump until it snapped. His father could not pay the smith. I ordered the boy to carry water each morning to the six households of Pump Court until the handle was mended, and I asked the smith not to hurry.

By the end he knew every old woman in the court by name, and one of them later left him her clock. I do not promise that every sentence ends in a clock.

volumes.title: On Being Unsure
volumes.text:
You will give rulings you never feel sure of. I, Dorcas Thrale, magistrate of Emberwick, set mine down for you, my successor, honestly.

Twenty years ago, on a night of hard frost, a girl of ten named Tamsin Reed unbolted the borough pound and let out three stray donkeys. They were cold, she told me, and the pound had no roof. By morning they were in the churchyard, having eaten a wreath. The law was plain. I fined her father two shillings and had her apologise to the pound-keeper.

She did, clearly. Then she looked at me a long moment, not angrily, but like someone working out a sum. I have wondered ever since what answer she got. I paid for a roof on the pound that spring and told nobody. Whether that was justice or only a conscience with a little money, I leave to you.

volumes.title: On the Kettle
volumes.text:
In the retiring room behind the bench at Emberwick there is a kettle. I, your predecessor, commend it to you as the most useful instrument of justice in the borough, the gavel not excepted.

When both parties have said the same thing three times, adjourn for ten minutes. People cannot keep up a fury while waiting for water to boil. The brothers Abel and Enoch Farr once came before me over their late mother's dresser, each ready to see it sawn in half sooner than yield. I put the kettle on and left the door ajar. Before it sang I heard Enoch say the thing would never go up his stairs anyway.

Abel took the dresser and Enoch took the plates that stood on it. Buy your own tea, by the way. The borough's allowance is poor stuff, and a ruling made on weak tea shows it.

volumes.title: On Witnesses
volumes.text:
Three sorts of witness want care, and in thirty-one years on the Emberwick bench I have met them all. Children tell the truth, but not always about the question you asked; ask again, differently. The very old remember the day wonderfully and the year not at all.

Beware most the witness who is sure of the hour. Ask instead what they were doing. "I had just taken the bread out" is worth more than "precisely ten past four".

A man once swore before me that he saw a cart at nine exactly, by the market clock. So he had. The market clock had stood at nine for a fortnight, waiting for the clockmaker. He was not lying. He had looked at a clock. Most false evidence is of that kind, successor: decent folk trusting stopped clocks. Be gentle with it, and send someone to check the clock.

volumes.title: On the Statute Book
volumes.text:
The Borough Clerk of Emberwick keeps the Statute Book, some forty by-laws. Read it through once, successor, then ask the Clerk how each one came about. Every statute was written by tired people one evening, to stop one particular nuisance happening twice.

There is a by-law against whistling near the weir after dusk. It dates from when the lock-keeper signalled the barges by whistle. A homesick drover from the Northern Fells was brought before me for whistling there to his dog. The fine is a shilling. The reason for the fine had been dead forty years.

I fined him the shilling, as I must. Then I paid him a shilling to carry a parcel to the bridge. You will be told this is not how the law works. In a town this size it is how it works best: the letter kept, and the purpose kept in mind.

volumes.title: On Tempers
volumes.text:
Anger will come into your court at Emberwick, as it came into mine. Do not raise your voice against it. Lower it. People must grow quiet to hear what is being said about them. And never rule while anyone is standing who ought to sit.

Two fishwives of the Grey Coast once came before me over a spilled barrow of mackerel, each with a row of cousins in the public seats. The Moot Room sounded like a gull colony. I said, very softly, that I would hear whoever sat down first. Then I had the usher open a window. The smell of roasting chestnuts came up from the market, and somebody's stomach spoke. They agreed to share the loss before noon.

Anger is mostly weather, successor. Wait, and it changes. So does your own. On a morning when you are cross, hear the small cases first.

volumes.title: On the Third Time
volumes.text:
The same faces return. Old Bartle Finch stood before me, I think, fourteen times in my years as magistrate of Emberwick, always for borrowing a boat that was not his to fish the Ember by night. He always brought it back by morning, clean, with a trout left in the bottom by way of rent.

Mercy is easy the first time. By the third, successor, you must ask whether you are being merciful or merely tired. Here is my test. Mercy costs you some thought. Laziness costs nothing.

So at last I thought, and asked him why he owned no boat. He had nowhere to keep one. I spoke to the ferryman, who now lets him a mooring for a trout a month. Bartle has not been before me since. I miss him. That too you will find: some of them you will miss.

volumes.title: On Clearing the Drawer
volumes.text:
The Midwinter Sessions are next week, my last, and I, Dorcas Thrale, have been emptying the bench drawer of thirty-one years. Nine pencils. A marble taken in evidence and never claimed. The receipt for a roof on the borough pound. I leave you the goose cushion, the kettle and this book.

The council meets tomorrow to name you. The market says an advocate from the Lowlands circuit. I find I mind more than I expected. The quarrels of Emberwick are a kind of garden, and I should like to know who is to have the watering of it.

One thing more stays in the drawer: a slip of paper reading "Tamsin Reed. Donkeys, frost, two shillings. Not sure." She was ten, and I fined her for a kindness. Every magistrate should leave the next one honest doubt. It keeps the chair from growing any taller.

volumes.title: The Name on the Door
volumes.text:
They have painted my successor's name on the Moot Room door, and I know it. Tamsin Reed. The council chose the advocate from the Lowlands circuit, and she is the girl who let three cold donkeys out of the Emberwick pound twenty years ago, whom I fined two shillings and never forgot.

You called on me yesterday, so I may write "you" and mean somebody. You said that in court that day you were working out how a magistrate could plainly agree with a child and fine her all the same. It took you twenty years and many books, you said, and you have the answer now, mostly. You did not say what it is. Quite right. I had my turn.

So this companion is handed across a tea table and not left in a drawer. Last counsel: the chair is too high. I have left the cushion.

volumes.title: The Rhubarb Line
volumes.text:
I, Septimus Pim, clerk to the Emberwick Petty Sessions, open the record of Tull against Sorrel, which began in April with a fence.

Mr. Ambrose Tull, retired barge-master, of Barge Cottage, Hollow Lane, had pulled down the rotten palings between his garden and that of Miss Winifred Sorrel, retired schoolmistress, of Quince Cottage, and put up a fence six feet high. Miss Sorrel said it stood nine inches on her side. In evidence she offered her rhubarb, which now grew, undeniably, in Mr. Tull's garden.

Mr. Tull said he had built where the old fence stood. Miss Sorrel said the old fence had wandered. Nobody living, the magistrate found, knew where the line ran. The fence stays until a survey can be had. Mr. Tull is to hand the rhubarb back over it, stalk by stalk. They left by separate doors. I have started a large file.

volumes.title: The Hen Called Duchess
volumes.text:
Second hearing, in June, of Tull against Sorrel, neighbours of Hollow Lane, Emberwick, recorded by me, Septimus Pim, clerk of the court. The complaint was not the fence between them, but what went under it.

Mr. Tull's hen, Duchess, has been squeezing beneath the new fence to lay in Miss Sorrel's woodpile. Miss Sorrel has been eating the eggs. Mr. Tull claimed eleven eggs or their value. Miss Sorrel replied that an egg laid on her land, by a trespasser, is rent. She added that no hen could get under the old fence, and whose fence was the new one?

The magistrate held that the hen is Tull's, the woodpile Sorrel's, and the egg a joint production. Eggs are to be shared alternately, and Mr. Tull is to stop the gap. He has done so, with a brick. Duchess has since been seen going over the top.

volumes.title: Sunflowers of Unusual Size
volumes.text:
Third hearing, in August, between Mr. Ambrose Tull and Miss Winifred Sorrel over the fence dividing their gardens in Hollow Lane, Emberwick. I, Septimus Pim, clerk, record it.

Miss Sorrel had planted seven sunflowers along her side. They now stood twelve feet high and had Mr. Tull's runner beans in shade from two o'clock. A statute limits fences to six feet. Mr. Tull called the sunflowers a fence by other means. Miss Sorrel, formerly a schoolmistress, said a sunflower is a flower, and produced a labelled diagram.

The magistrate held that a sunflower is not a fence and shade is not trespass. She then observed, having walked out to look, that all seven flowers had turned their faces over the fence towards Mr. Tull, so that he had the best of them and Miss Sorrel the backs. No order was made. Miss Sorrel went home thoughtful.

volumes.title: The Quince Jelly Question
volumes.text:
In October the quarrel of Hollow Lane came a fourth time before the Emberwick bench, and I, Septimus Pim, clerk, took it down. The fence between Mr. Tull and Miss Sorrel stood as before. This time the trouble came over it.

Miss Sorrel's quince tree overhangs Mr. Tull's garden, and its windfalls land there. He had made eleven jars of jelly from them. Miss Sorrel claimed the jelly. Mr. Tull said fruit that falls on his ground is his, and the sugar was certainly his.

The magistrate tasted the exhibit, twice. She ruled that by old custom fallen fruit belongs where it lands. No law compels a gift, though manners suggest a jar. Mr. Tull set a jar on my table and said the court might do as it liked. The court handed it to Miss Sorrel. She said it wanted more lemon, and took it home.

volumes.title: Two Coats of Paint
volumes.text:
Fifth hearing of Tull against Sorrel, neighbours in Hollow Lane, Emberwick; Septimus Pim, clerk, recording. In a dry week of November Mr. Tull painted his side of the fence barge green. The paint ran through the gaps and striped Miss Sorrel's side. She painted her side white. The white ran through and striped his. The fence now resembled a humbug, and each sued the other for spoiling it.

The magistrate ruled that each face of a fence belongs to the eye obliged to look at it. Each may paint their own side their own colour. While one paints, the other must stand behind and hold a board across the gaps.

It took a whole Saturday, I am told, and words passed between the boards, not all hostile. Miss Sorrel informed Mr. Tull, through a knothole, that he had missed a bit. He went back and did it.

volumes.title: The Surveyor's Chain
volumes.text:
In December the long case of Tull against Sorrel, concerning the fence between their gardens in Hollow Lane, at last had its survey. I, Septimus Pim, clerk of the Emberwick court, attended with the file, which now needs string.

Mr. Linus Rood, borough surveyor, laid out his chain. Mr. Tull's deed measures forty feet from the lane. Miss Sorrel's measures thirty feet from the brook. But the brook has moved since the deeds were written. By his deed the fence stands correctly. By hers it stands nine inches wrong. Both deeds speak of a mere-stone, a boundary stone between the plots, and nobody can find it. Mr. Rood probed with a rod and found a drain and a horseshoe.

The magistrate could not choose between two honest deeds and one dishonest brook. The matter stands over until the stone is found. Each told me this proved their case.

volumes.title: Whose Snow
volumes.text:
January brought the seventh hearing between Mr. Tull of Barge Cottage and Miss Sorrel of Quince Cottage, Emberwick, whose gardens share a fence and little else. I, Septimus Pim, clerk, record it. Snow had slid from Mr. Tull's shed roof onto Miss Sorrel's path. She shovelled it back over the fence. He returned it, with interest. By my reckoning the same snow crossed six times.

The magistrate ruled that snow is nobody's property until it lies in the lane, where it becomes the borough's. Both were ordered to shovel it out to the lane together, under my eye.

I attended in two scarves. The work took twenty minutes. Afterwards the parties stood either side of the fence disputing the right way to hold a shovel, for forty minutes more, neither going indoors. I record this without comment, except that I went home before they did.

volumes.title: Bonfires and Bed Linen
volumes.text:
Eighth hearing, in March, of Tull against Sorrel, the neighbours of Hollow Lane, Emberwick, and their fence; taken down by me, Septimus Pim, clerk. Mr. Tull had burned his prunings on the morning Miss Sorrel hung out her sheets. She washed them again. A pillowcase then blew over the fence and settled in his ashes. He complained that her linen had trespassed. She answered that his smoke had trespassed first.

The magistrate sent for an almanac and drew up a calendar. Mondays are for washing. Thursdays are for bonfires. A copy was to be pinned to each side of the fence.

Mr. Tull objected that he could not see her copy to know whether it matched his. I was made to certify both. It is the first document the two have ever held in common, and I wrote it out rather well.

volumes.title: The Trowel in Common
volumes.text:
In May the neighbours of Hollow Lane, Mr. Tull and Miss Sorrel, came a ninth time before the Emberwick bench. I, Septimus Pim, clerk, expected the fence. It was a trowel with a red handle, which each said the other had kept.

Under questioning it came out that for eleven years, before Mr. Tull built his six-foot fence, the two had passed tools, seedlings and opinions across the old low palings daily. Nobody knew whose the trowel was, because it had lived on the fence post. The magistrate asked what the quarrel was truly about. Nobody spoke. At last Miss Sorrel said the old fence came up to her elbow, and that she is five feet two. Mr. Tull looked at his boots.

The trowel is to hang on the fence, in a hole cut so that both may reach it. I begin to understand my file.

volumes.title: The Leaning Fence
volumes.text:
Tenth hearing, in August, of Tull against Sorrel; Septimus Pim, clerk to the Emberwick sessions, recording. The fence between the two gardens in Hollow Lane now leans towards Miss Sorrel under the weight of Mr. Tull's runner beans. She has propped it with clothes poles. He complained that her props push it back upon his beans.

The magistrate remarked that this fence has appeared before her more often than any person in the borough. She added that a fence held up by two people, each wishing it to fall the other way, is likely to stand for ever. Each is to prop their own side.

A hole was cut in the fence last spring so that both might reach a shared trowel. A good deal now passes through it: runner beans one way, and the other way a slice of something with quince in it.

volumes.title: The Night of the Gale
volumes.text:
In October a gale laid the fence of Hollow Lane flat across both gardens, impartially. Mr. Tull and Miss Sorrel each came to the Emberwick bench to blame the other for not holding it up, and I, Septimus Pim, clerk, opened the file for the eleventh time.

The evidence overtook them. Digging out the snapped post, Mr. Tull's spade had rung on stone: the lost boundary stone, a foot down, a cross cut in its top. Mr. Rood, the surveyor, measured from it. The true boundary lies four and a half inches from where the fence stood, halfway between the line Mr. Tull swore to and the line Miss Sorrel swore to. Each had been half right for eighteen months.

The magistrate reserved her ruling and advised both to consider what fence they wanted on that line. It was raining. For once they left by the same door.

volumes.title: Settled Over the Fence
volumes.text:
At the November sessions in Emberwick the case of Tull against Sorrel was called three times and nobody answered. The magistrate sent me, Septimus Pim, clerk, to Hollow Lane to see why.

I found both parties in the gap where the old six-foot fence blew down. They were setting posts along the line of the boundary stone, for a fence no higher than an elbow, with a gate in the middle. Mr. Tull was digging. Miss Sorrel held the post plumb and told him it was not. He said they had no time for court, with frost coming. She said the rhubarb had been moved back, and that he had moved it.

A jar of quince jelly stood on the stone. I have written across the file: settled out of court, over the fence. The magistrate says she will miss them. Duchess the hen uses the gate.
